source.verse_hash_method: SHA-256 of exact tab-separated Greek payload, retaining whitespace and variant markers.

notes: The wording ‘the rest of humanity’ follows the Greek form of Amos used in the speech.
The four requirements are retained as listed in the pinned text; their later application requires contextual reading.
Public verse 34 is absent from the pinned Greek text, so the numbering moves from 33 to 35.
The girl is enslaved, exploited for profit, and then disappears from the account after liberation from the spirit. The translation preserves both spiritual and economic harm.
Paul and Silas invoke Roman citizenship after being beaten publicly without trial.
‘Babbler’ literally evokes a seed-picker and functions as a dismissive insult.
The description can mean very religious or superstitious; Paul begins with an observation rather than a simple compliment.
Paul quotes language familiar from Greek poets while directing the argument toward the Creator.
Claudius’s expulsion order is the narrator’s historical explanation for Aquila and Priscilla’s move.
The pinned text names Priscilla before Aquila while both explain the way of God to Apollos.
The narrative reports extraordinary healings associated with cloths and work aprons; it does not establish a commodity or technique.
The men flee naked and wounded after severe physical violence.
The object ‘fallen from heaven’ is left as the city clerk’s conventional claim about Artemis’s image.
Public verse 41 is absent from the pinned Greek numbering; its dismissal sentence is included at the end of verse 40.
vocabulary: Way; here a name for the Jesus movement.

notes: ‘The first day of the week’ names the gathering’s day; breaking bread can carry both meal and communal worship associations.
The phrase translated ‘the blood of his own Son’ is literally ‘the blood of his own’ and is grammatically difficult.
Paul preserves a saying of Jesus not recorded in the four Gospels.
The Spirit-given warnings name the suffering ahead; the narrative also records Paul’s resolve and the community’s submission to the Lord’s will.
Philip’s four unmarried daughters are explicitly prophets.
The pinned text contains all four requirements, including abstention from food offered to idols.
vocabulary: Evangelist or proclaimer of good news.

notes: The companions see the light but do not understand the voice; the translation distinguishes hearing a sound from comprehending speech.
The threatened flogging and Paul’s Roman citizenship are stated as legal and bodily realities.
Baptism, washing, sins, and calling on the name appear together without the note imposing a later ritual theory.
vocabulary: Righteous or just; here a title.

notes: Paul says he did not know Ananias was high priest; the text does not explain why.
‘Both’ gathers the disputed realities of angel and spirit alongside resurrection; the concise Greek need not define their relation.
The escort comprises two hundred infantry, seventy cavalry, and two hundred spearmen.
vocabulary: A soldier described by a rare term, probably a spearman or light-armed guard.

notes: Public verse 7 is absent from the pinned Greek text, so the numbering moves from 6 to 8.
Paul accepts the name ‘the Way’ while rejecting its dismissal as merely a sect.
Drusilla is named, identified as Felix’s wife, and identified as Jewish.
Paul accepts death if a capital offense is proved but refuses political surrender and appeals to Caesar.
Festus describes the dispute from his own outsider perspective; ‘a dead man named Jesus’ is his characterization, not the narrator’s conclusion.
vocabulary: Augustus or emperor, an imperial title.

notes: ‘Kick against the goads’ is a proverb for futile resistance to forceful direction.
The commission uses sight, darkness and light, dominion, forgiveness, and inheritance imagery together.
Agrippa’s phrase can be heard as a question or assertion about a short time; the main text makes the rhetorical force explicit without claiming certainty.
‘Sea anchor’ renders a general gear term whose exact nautical referent is uncertain.
The pinned text numbers everyone aboard as 276 people.
The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners; the centurion prevents it because he wants to save Paul.
The Greek calls the islanders ‘barbarians,’ meaning non-Greek-speaking people; the main text uses the neutral description ‘local people.’
The Twin Gods are Castor and Pollux, the ship’s pagan emblem.
Public verse 29 is absent from the pinned Greek text, so the numbering moves from 28 to 30.
